title: Evolution and Natural Selection
summary: This lesson explains how variation and adaptation drive evolution and presents the main lines of evidence that support it. Students will learn why natural selection is a powerful mechanism shaping life on Earth.

sections.heading: Variation Within Populations
sections.body:
Individuals of the same species are not identical. Differences in size, colour, behaviour, or physiology are called variation, and they arise from mutations, gene shuffling during reproduction, and environmental influences.

Variation is crucial because it provides the raw material for natural selection. Without differences, no trait could be favoured or discarded over time.

sections.heading: Adaptation and Natural Selection
sections.body:
An adaptation is a trait that improves an organism's chance of surviving and reproducing in its environment. Natural selection works like a filter: individuals with beneficial adaptations are more likely to pass their genes to the next generation.

Over many generations, advantageous traits become more common, while harmful traits may disappear. This gradual change in the genetic makeup of a population is evolution.

sections.heading: Evidence for Evolution
sections.body:
Scientists use several lines of evidence to show that evolution has occurred. Fossil records reveal a chronological succession of life forms, showing how simple organisms gave rise to more complex ones.

Comparative anatomy (e.g., the similar bone structure of a human hand, a bat wing, and a whale flipper) and molecular data (DNA similarities) demonstrate common ancestry. Biogeography, the study of species distribution, also supports evolution, as isolated islands often host unique, closely related species.

key_terms.meaning: Differences in traits among individuals of the same species.
A trait that increases an organism's fitness in its environment.
The process where individuals with advantageous traits reproduce more successfully.
Preserved remains of past organisms that show changes over geological time.
Body parts in different species that share a common ancestry but may have different functions.

quiz.q: What provides the raw material for natural selection?
quiz.why: Natural selection acts on existing variation within a population.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of an adaptation?
options: A random mutation that does not affect survival
quiz.why: The long neck helps giraffes reach food, increasing their survival and reproduction.

quiz.q: Which line of evidence compares DNA sequences between species?
quiz.why: Molecular biology examines genetic similarities that reveal common ancestry.

options: The distribution of species across Earth
quiz.why: Biogeography looks at where species live and how geography influences evolution.

flashcards.back: Differences in traits among individuals of the same species.
A trait that improves an organism's ability to survive and reproduce.

flashcards.front: Explain natural selection in one sentence.
flashcards.back: It is the process where individuals with beneficial traits leave more offspring, spreading those traits.

flashcards.front: Name one type of evidence for evolution.
flashcards.back: Fossil record, comparative anatomy, molecular data, or biogeography.
Similar body parts in different species that come from a common ancestor.
